Case study 02 · Olyv Plus · Android

Improving Loan & CC Management System UX on Olyv

Olyv Plus helps users track their complete credit profile, including loans and credit cards. The section was already there, but the drop-offs couldn't be ignored. A few iterations, field testing, and several espresso shots later, we found the version that made sense to our users.

What is Olyv Plus

₹39 a month. Your credit profile, all in one place.

Olyv Plus is a subscription that shows you your credit score, tracks your active loans and credit cards pulled from bureau data, and gives you tools to dispute errors or improve your score. The loan management section was the most visited part — and the most confusing.

🛒

Paan shopkeeper

Took a loan for inventory and wanted to check his EMI due date. Got confused by the sheer number of categories.

🔒

Security guard

Had a personal loan from Bajaj Finance, saw the Home Loan category and tapped it — thinking he might get a home loan from Olyv.

🍊

🥛

🍽️

💼

Salaried worker

Just wants to keep track of his loan EMI payments regularly.

Before the redesign

Built around categories, not the user's loans

To check a single loan, a user had to go through four separate screens. Every step added friction — and the worst part was step two, where they were shown every loan category that exists, whether or not they actually had a loan in it.

Current problems
To check one loan, a user tapped through four screens — and got shown every category along the way, whether they had a loan in it or not.

The core problem: showing every category — even empty ones — deviated the user's intent. Someone who came to check their personal loan had to wade past home loans, gold loans, and schemes they'd never touched. By the time they reached their loan, they'd lost the thread.

Research

I stopped guessing and went to where the users were

There was no point theorising about what was wrong. The people using Olyv Plus aren't in offices — they're behind shop counters and at railway-station kiosks in Bengaluru. So I went to them. Research ran across three methods, each answering a different question.

Method 01
Street testing in Kadubeesanahalli

I walked up to real users at their shops and workplaces around Kadubeesanahalli and Panathur — a paan shop, a general store near the railway station — and asked if they'd open Olyv and try to find their loan while I watched. Most agreed. I recorded the sessions on my phone with their consent so I could go back and study exactly where they hesitated, mis-tapped, or gave up.

Watching someone use the app in their own hands, in their own environment, showed me things no analytics dashboard could. The confusion was physical — you could see them pause, scroll back up, re-read a category name, and tap the wrong thing.

On-site at a store near Panathur Railway Station, Panathur
A user navigating the old flow on his own phone
Watching where users tapped first, and where they stalled
1Users tapped category names like "Home Loan" expecting to apply for one — not to see their existing loans.

"He tapped on Home Loan expecting to apply for one. Spent two minutes on the screen before he realised it was showing his existing loans — not offering him a new one. He didn't go back in."

Street testing, Kadubeesanahalli · Security guard · Personal loan with HDFC
Method 02
Microsoft Clarity session recordings

Street testing told me why users struggled. Clarity told me how often, and at scale. I went through session recordings, heatmaps, and scroll-depth data for the loan section — watching anonymised replays of how hundreds of real users moved through the flow.

The recordings surfaced patterns I couldn't get from a handful of in-person sessions: rage taps on non-interactive elements, users abandoning the flow at the category page, and dead scrolls where people hunted for a loan that was buried deep in the list.

Method 03
Phone calls with real users

Finally, I called some of the users I'd spotted struggling in the Clarity recordings. I wanted to hear, in their own words, what they'd been trying to do and whether they'd managed it. These conversations confirmed what I'd seen and added the language users actually use when they talk about their own money.

The recurring theme: people think in terms of their bank and how much they owe — "my HDFC loan," "the ₹1.2 lakh one" — never in terms of loan categories. That single insight shaped the entire redesign.

7Users described loans by bank name and amount, never by category.

Prioritisation
What we found, and what we chose to fix

Via research, I found a few issues in the existing flow that were then validated after watching Clarity Videos. I added everything to a Figjam File and discussed with PM what issues to fix, after marking critical ones.

Fixed in this version
Backlogged due to time consumption
Will be picked later due to tech constraint
Category names were being read as loan offers, not loan types
Users tapped "Home Loan" expecting to apply for one. Olyv doesn't offer home loans. This wasn't a fringe case — it happened in almost every street session.
Street testing · Clarity recordings
Fixed
Users couldn't recognise their own loan in the category view
Nobody thinks "I have a personal loan" — they think "I have an HDFC loan for ₹1.2L." Category labels had no meaning. Bank name and amount are how people remember their loans.
Street testing · User calls
Fixed
Two taps to see a loan, and a blank screen if you didn't have that type
Category → intermediate page → loan list. If you tapped "Education Loan" and didn't have one, you got a blank screen with no explanation. Users assumed the app was broken.
Clarity rage taps · Street testing
Fixed
Olyv Plus homepage gave users no reason to tap into the loan section
Six benefit cards, all equal size, none personalised. Users with 3 active loans had no idea they were there — the homepage never told them. Entry point was invisible.
Clarity scroll depth · User calls
Fixed
Loan card showed outstanding amount inconsistently — sometimes Lakhs, sometimes full number
"45 Lacs" on one card, "25000" on another. No formatting standard. Users found it hard to compare two loans at a glance.
Street testing
Fixed
No way to know EMI due date from the list view
The most common reason users opened the section was to check "when is my EMI due." That date wasn't visible until two taps in. Most gave up before reaching it.
User calls · Clarity
Backlogged
Credit card section had no indication of how much was available to spend
Users wanted "how much can I still use" — the card showed total limit and limit utilised, but not available balance. Made users do subtraction in their head.
Street testing · User calls
Backlogged
No search or filter on the loan list
Users with 4+ loans had to scroll through all of them. A search by bank name or a filter by loan type would have made it faster — especially for users with multiple loans from the same bank.
User calls
Tech constraint
Bureau data refresh lag made some loans show stale information
Experian and CIBIL data was sometimes weeks old, but the app showed it without any staleness indicator. Users didn't know if what they were seeing was current.

The issues we decided to fix were the ones causing the most drop-offs and led to user confusion.

Design decisions

What I changed, and the thinking behind each one

Decision 01
Show bank name and loan amount first — not the loan category
Why the old way failed

Cards led with category — "Home Loans: 3". To find your loan, you first had to know which category it was in. Most users couldn't. In testing, people with a Bajaj personal loan tapped "Auto Loan" because they associated Bajaj with the brand, not the category.

What we did instead

Every card now leads with bank name + amount — "HDFC Bank · ₹1,20,000". Loan type moves below as secondary info.

  • Bank name — how users identify their lender
  • Amount — how they remember what they borrowed
  • EMI per month — what they check most often
Decision 02
Remove the category layer entirely — show all loans on one screen
Why the old way failed

The flow was category grid → tap category → see loans. Two taps before any real data — and tapping an empty category showed a blank screen. In Clarity, this was the biggest source of rage taps.

What we did instead

All loans on one scrollable list, no category page. Two loans from different banks in the same category simply both show up, told apart by bank and amount. The blank screen can't happen anymore — you either have loans or you don't.

Decision 03
Replace the Olyv Plus benefits grid with personalised entry points
Why the old way failed

The homepage was a 6-card benefits grid, all equal weight, all pointing to features. Nothing signalled the user had loans waiting inside. Clarity showed most people scrolled right past.

What we did instead

The homepage now surfaces the user's own numbers as entry points: "2 Active Loans" and "3 Active Credit Cards." The moment you see your own count, the intent to tap is obvious.

This was the most iterated thing in the whole project. The homepage went through more rounds than the loan section itself. We tried credit score first, overdue amounts, a summary card — nothing pulled users in like showing them their own loan count.
Decision 04
Remove loan categories from the app homepage entirely
Why it needed to change

The app homepage had the same category grid (Home, Auto, Gold, Personal). Users hit it earlier in the journey and tried to apply for loans, because the category names read like offer buttons.

What we did instead

Replaced the grid with plain counts — "2 Active Loans", "3 Active Credit Cards" — and dropped the decorative 3D illustrations. Label, count, arrow. Nothing to misread.

Decision 05
Standardise how outstanding amounts are formatted
Why the old way failed

Amounts had no formatting standard — one card said "45 Lacs", the next "25000". Users couldn't glance and compare two loans, which is exactly what they came to do.

What we did instead

One consistent format everywhere — ₹ with grouped digits ("₹1,20,000"). Same style on every card, every screen, so amounts line up and read at a glance.

After the redesign

What it looked like after

Four surfaces changed — the app homepage, the Olyv Plus homepage, the loan accounts summary, and the individual loan detail page. Each now leads with what the user actually came to see.

◆ The entry point
Your own numbers, right on the homepage

The category grid is gone. In its place, the homepage now shows "2 Active Loans" and "3 Active Credit Cards" with real balances — the single change that moved section visits the most.

Personalised counts replace generic category cards
Outstanding balance shown upfront — no tap needed
One clear tap into the section they came for
Olyv Plus homepage
Benefits reframed around the user

The flat 6-card benefits grid was replaced with a credit-first layout — score, recommended actions, and a clear credit summary that surfaces loans and cards instead of burying them under equal-weight feature tiles.

Credit score and summary lead the page
Loans and cards surfaced, not hidden in a grid
Loan accounts summary
Every loan on one screen, led by the bank

No more category maze. All loans sit in a single list — bank name and amount first, loan type as a secondary tag. Active and Closed split into tabs, with a real total at the top.

Bank name + amount lead every row
Category demoted to a small tag, not a page
Active / Closed tabs replace the long scroll
Total amount and loan counts summarised up top
Loan detail page
Far more the user can actually do

The detail page went from a dead-end to a genuinely useful screen. It now carries payment history, downloadable documents, full loan details, and support — everything a user might need about that one loan, in one place.

12-month payment history at a glance

Nobody planned for the DSA number

Future prospects

What I want to pick up in the next revamp

A few things couldn't make this cycle — some blocked by tech constraints, some by time. These are the ones I want to take on next.

Search and filter on the loan list

Users with four or more loans still have to scroll. A search by bank name and a filter by loan type would make finding one loan instant — especially for users with several loans from the same lender.

Blocked by tech constraint

A freshness indicator on bureau data

Experian and CIBIL data can be weeks old, but the app shows it without any signal. A "last updated" state would tell users whether what they're seeing is current before they act on it.

Blocked by tech constraint

Available-to-spend on credit cards

The card view shows total limit and utilised, but not what's left — so users do the maths themselves. Surfacing available balance directly is a small change with a real everyday payoff.

Deprioritised for time

EMI due dates on the list view

The most common reason people open the section is to check when an EMI is due — but that's buried two taps deep. Bringing the next due date onto the list itself would answer the top question at a glance.

Deprioritised for time
